# Draft:Southampton - World War 2 Second Front

Major General Sir Nigel (Noel) Holmes speaking in 1945 said, 'Without Southampton we could not have done D-Day' (The English Gateway, Bernard Knowles, 1951). However his words are rarely believed because most people associate Southwick Park north of Portsmouth with the headquarters for D Day. However Portsmouth was only the titular headquarters. D Day rehearsals, for example at Slapton Sands, proved to Admiral Ramsay that if the landings were going to succeed the invasion fleet would need, 'close and continuous control'.
Staff Sargent Irwin Swerdlow in his article for the Army Transportation Journal Vol. 1, No. 9 (October, 1945), pp. 23-25 said,
'Early in May, a month before D-Day, Southampton and its litter of sub-ports became the focus in the preparation for the great outbound movement to the continent. These sub-ports, operated by the 14th Port with headquarters at Southampton, included Portland, Weymouth, Truro, Plymouth, Falmouth, Dartmouth, Hayle, Totnes, Hamble, and Poole'.
Above the doorway to the Art Gallery rooms in the Civic Centre which were used as the US Army headquarters on D-Day there is a plaque that says,
'Presented by the 14th Major Port US Army in acknowledgement of the generosity of the Borough of Southampton which during the mayoralty of Rex Stranger MC gratuitously provided the section of the Civic Center for use as headquarters for the port. It was from here that orders emanated directing the movement of the vast American armies through Southampton and other South Coast ports between June 1944 and the end of hostilities in the great war for the liberation of Europe'.
The word 'gratuitously' was added as an in-joke between allies because there was some discussion at the time about whether the US Army should pay rent for using the rooms.
Outside the entrance to the Art Gallery where a GI once stood on guard there is another plaque which reads,
'This tablet records that a wing of the Civic Center was used as headquarters by the 14th Major Port US Army during World War II. Between D-Day, June 6th and the end of hostilities orders were issued from here directing the embarkation of American Armies who together with their Allies sailed from Southampton Docks to liberate Europe. During the operation over 2,250,000 troops 250,000 vehicles and millions of tons of supplies of the US Army were shipped through this port'.
Many people do not realise that the 14th Major Port was the US Army designation for the unit that was responsible for 'planning and directing' US forces on D Day and during Operation Overlord.
The two names on the World War Two plaques include Colonel Sherman L Kiser, US Regular Army, who received a CBE. He was posted, on 10 June 1944, to the Joint British and US Marshalling staff of Area “C”; since 23 July 1944 he held the appointment of Commander 14 Major Port, Southampton. His citation reads,
'During the Build Up, both American and British Forces were using the Port of Southampton, the troops of both nations often using the same Marshalling and Transit Camps and the greatest co-ordination was necessary to ensure the essential smooth working in the Camps, on the Hards and in the Docks. Both during the Build Up and since, the liaison and co-operation between the British and American Forces in the Southampton Area have been excellent. To a very large extent this result is due to the personal efforts of Colonel Kiser, who at all times has done his utmost to further the combined operations in this area. He has always been most anxious to co-operate and his relations with the Royal Navy, police, Local authorities, Southern Railway and Harbour Board have been equally cordial and helpful'. (National Archives Reference WO 373/152/406).
The other name on the plaque is Colonel Leo J Meyer, US Army Reserve, who was awarded an OBE. He was posted to the headquarters at Southampton on 28 February 44 and appointed Port Commander on 29 May 1944. On 25 July, when the 14 Port was re-organised, he was appointed deputy to the senior officer. His citation reads,
'During the whole of this period, Colonel Meyer has worked in the closest touch with the British Army. His willing and untiring efforts to do all in his power to further the common cause has been most marked. Undoubtedly his able co-operation has done a great deal of good in cementing the good feeling between both the Military and Civil Authorities in this area'. (National Archives Reference WO 373/152/443)
Most people associate Portsmouth as the traditional home of the Royal Navy with D Day but in 1944 all the capital ships were moved to Scapa Flow for safety and it was the premier civilian passenger and ferry port with a double high tide that allowed landing craft to berth at any time of the tide that was the real home of D Day.
In 1946 Southampton recognised the crucial role of the 14th Major Port, United States Army Transportation Corps, with soldiers marching through the Bargate to receive the Honorary Freedom of the Borough, cementing the vital wartime link with American forces.
